newsitem.title: USA: Hun Sen's coup derailed peace ceremony: Post.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen's coup derailed peace ceremony: Post.

text.p: A ceremony to announce a truce between Khmer Rouge guerrillas and Cambodia's government was only a day away when Second Prime Minister Hun Sen seized power by ousting his rival and co-premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh, the Washington Post reported on Sunday.

The newspaper said it had obtained government documents signed by Khmer Rouge negotiators showing that on July 4 the guerrillas finally agreed to integrate their troops into the army and recognize the government.
Plans were made to announce the deal in a ceremony scheduled for July 6, according to the report.
Instead, Hun Sen, apparently fearing the peace agreement was a ploy to weaken him militarily and politically, launched a coup July 5 to scuttle it, the Post said.
Within 48 hours Hun Sen had inflicted a total defeat on Ranariddh's forces in the capital, Phnom Penh.

The agreement, principally between Ranariddh and the Khmer Rouge's nominal leader, Khieu Samphan, was the culmination of a score of secret meetings between Khmer Rouge leaders and government military negotiators.
The guerrillas agreed in principle to integrate their army into the government armed forces, recognize the Cambodian constitution and formally disband their "provisional government," the Post said.

By July 3, both sides had hammered out all details of the agreement. A statement that was to be announced on the radio and read by Khieu Samphan at a press conference on July 6 was signed by both sides, including Ranariddh on behalf of the government, the newspaper said.

The Washington Post report was written by American journalist Nate Thayer, a correspondent with the Far Eastern Economic Review who witnessed the show trial of reviled Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot last month.
Pol Pot was the architect of the Khmer Rouge's "killing fields" rule from 1975-79 during which more than a million Cambodians died from execution, torture, disease, starvation or hard labor.
Bitter disagreement over how to handle the Khmer Rouge between Hun Sen and Ranariddh was a key factor leading to Hun Sen's ouster of his co-premier.
